Why Multi-Unit Properties Need an Electrical Support Program

Bulk utility billing gives owners one invoice and little control over the information behind it. A manager may know the building's total electricity cost without knowing which suites drive consumption, how much power common areas use, or whether a resident's charge reflects actual usage.

That information gap becomes a staffing cost. Managers may compare occupancy records, move-in dates, estimated allocations, and utility statements to answer routine disputes. If the distribution system never produced suite-level data, that effort still cannot produce a reliable explanation.

How an Electrical Support Program Works
Think of an electrical support program as a
utility operating system for the building
. The meters are the sensors, the data layer carries readings, the billing engine applies the approved rules, and the dashboard gives people a usable view of what the system is reporting.

The physical installation comes first. A provider assesses the electrical distribution, confirms which suites and common areas require measurement, selects compliant equipment, and coordinates the installation with electricians and property staff. The design must reflect the building's wiring, access conditions, jurisdiction, and billing method rather than relying on a generic equipment package.

body.alt: A diagram illustrating the four layers of an electrical support program for building utility management systems.

children.text: Four connected layers
Layer one is measurement.

Approved submeters record the electricity assigned to each unit or designated load. Common-area metering helps distinguish elevators, corridors, mechanical rooms, and other shared consumption from suite usage where the building configuration supports that separation.
Layer two is data collection.

A communications hub receives readings and moves them into the operating platform. The provider should define how missing data, communication interruptions, meter faults, and unusual readings are identified and escalated.
Layer three is billing.

The billing system converts validated readings into monthly statements. It should account for account changes, move-ins, move-outs, exceptions, adjustments, collections workflows, and resident support. Billing accuracy depends on the quality of the meter data and the rules applied to it.
Layer four is visibility.

Owners and managers need reporting that helps them review consumption, identify irregularities, monitor common areas, and answer tenant questions. Residents benefit when their statements explain what they're being charged for instead of presenting an unexplained allocation.
Property teams managing installation work across multiple trades can also benefit from structured
field service in Dynamics 365
, particularly when work orders, technician activity, site access, and follow-up tasks need a common record.
For a visual explanation of the operating flow, review
how utility submetering works

. The important question isn't whether a platform has a dashboard. It's whether the entire chain, from the electrical panel to the tenant's invoice, has an accountable owner and a documented control process.
What happens after commissioning

Commissioning confirms that the installed meters, communications, account mapping, and billing logic agree with the approved design. A responsible provider resolves discrepancies before live billing rather than asking residents to act as the testing department.

After launch, ongoing service matters just as much. Meters can lose communication, units can change occupants, and building electrical work can affect the measurement arrangement. The program should include a clear route for detecting issues, correcting data, maintaining equipment, and communicating with affected residents.
Benefits for Property Owners and Tenants

The value of measured billing appears differently on each side of the lease. Owners gain a clearer operating model, while tenants gain a more understandable relationship between consumption and charges.
For an owner, the first benefit is
cost recovery

. Instead of carrying a pooled electricity expense without suite-level information, the property can allocate eligible consumption according to measured usage and the approved billing structure. That improves budget visibility and gives management a more defensible basis for discussing utility charges.

The second benefit is operational control. Consumption reports can help a manager investigate unusual usage, review common-area loads, and identify where building improvements deserve attention. The data doesn't replace engineering analysis, but it gives the engineering and operations teams a better starting point.

body.alt: A comparison chart outlining the benefits of an electrical submetering program for property owners and tenants.

children.text: A more defensible tenant conversation

Consider two buildings with similar electricity costs. In the first, the manager sends a pooled or estimated charge and handles complaints through email. In the second, the resident receives a statement tied to a measured unit reading, with the billing period and account details clearly identified.

The second building hasn't eliminated every dispute. It has improved the quality of the conversation. Staff can investigate a specific reading or account event instead of defending an opaque allocation method.
For tenants, the main advantages are practical:
Fairer allocation:
Residents can understand why their charge differs from another suite's charge.
Better feedback:
Consumption information gives people a basis for changing habits or investigating appliances.
Fewer surprises:
Regular, measured statements are easier to plan for than unexplained adjustments.
Clearer responsibility:
The statement distinguishes the tenant's assigned usage from building-level or common-area costs where the billing design allows it.
When residents can connect a bill to a measured service, the manager's role shifts from defending the invoice to explaining the system.
The conservation effect matters at portfolio scale. The Ontario analysis cited earlier identifies approximately
eleven terawatt hours of cumulative technical potential over five years
from applying electricity sub-metering across applicable multi-residential units, supporting the view that measurement can create feedback loops beyond revenue allocation. The
Axis Meter Solutions case studies

can help property teams examine how metering programs fit into broader building operations, but owners should still test the design against their own electrical distribution and regulatory obligations.

A program also reduces administrative friction when the provider handles billing setup, collections workflows, resident support, maintenance, and meter replacement planning. The owner still needs governance and oversight, but the property team no longer has to assemble every function from separate vendors.
Regulatory and Licensing Requirements You Must Know

A submetering project can be installed correctly and still fail operationally if the billing structure, approvals, or provider responsibilities are unclear. In Ontario, unit sub-metering must involve a licensed Unit Sub-Meter Provider. The Ontario Energy Board's
Unit Sub-Metering Code
sets requirements for licensed providers, Measurement Canada standards, and the upstream interval principal meter arrangement.
Start with the upstream meter

The principal consumer must request the interval principal meter, and the distributor must install it, before unit sub-metering begins. This sequence affects procurement, electrical work, commissioning, and billing activation. Installing suite meters before confirming the upstream condition can force redesign, delay occupancy or billing, and leave the owner exposed to disputes.
Before work starts, require the provider to document:
Principal meter status:
Confirm that the interval meter exists and supports the proposed arrangement.
Provider licence:
Verify that the provider is authorised for the applicable Ontario activity.
Meter selection:
Confirm that the equipment meets the required Measurement Canada standard.
Installation method:
Match the installation to the approved electrical design and actual site conditions.
Billing authority:
Define how charges will be calculated, communicated, corrected, and supported.
Commissioning evidence:
Retain records proving that the system was tested before live billing.

A licence number does not settle the compliance question. Ask what the licence covers, who coordinates approvals, how meter accuracy is validated, and who responds when a meter reading or billing record is challenged. Put those answers in the agreement, not only in meeting notes.
The compliance question is not “Can someone install a meter?” It's “Can this specific measurement and billing chain be installed, validated, and operated under the applicable rules?”
Jurisdiction changes the design

Ontario requirements do not automatically apply to properties in other provinces or states. A design may need different equipment, permits, inspections, account treatment, or tenant communications in another jurisdiction. Validate local requirements before procurement, electrical work, and contract signing.

Owners should define how the agreement handles regulatory updates, meter replacement, inspections, data retention, billing corrections, and disputes. Vague terms can transfer ongoing work to property staff without a budget, training, or clear escalation path.

For portfolios spanning several jurisdictions, maintain a site-by-site compliance register. Record the authority having jurisdiction, required approvals, electrical design status, installation records, commissioning documents, billing rules, responsible parties, and open issues. Review the register at each project milestone. It gives owners a practical audit trail and exposes unresolved regulatory work before it becomes a billing or tenant-service problem.
The $0 Upfront Model Versus Self-Managed Submetering

The decision isn't just whether to install submeters. It's whether the owner wants to own the equipment, process, compliance exposure, and service burden, or transfer those responsibilities under a long-term operating agreement.
In a
$0 upfront turnkey model
, the provider owns and maintains the equipment over a standard
20-year term

, as described in the program scope. The owner avoids an initial capital purchase and receives a bundled service that can include design, installation, commissioning, billing, reporting, maintenance, and meter replacement.

Self-managed submetering gives the owner more direct control, but that control comes with a long list of obligations. The property team must source compliant equipment, coordinate electricians, manage access, establish account mapping, purchase or build billing infrastructure, communicate with tenants, handle exceptions, maintain records, and respond when equipment or regulations change.

The turnkey approach isn't automatically right for every operator. An owner with established metering expertise, internal billing capability, and a strong compliance function may prefer direct control. But that owner should price the full operating workload, not just the meter purchase.
The

illustrates the type of structure owners should examine when comparing capital preservation with long-term service commitments. Review the agreement for term, ownership, maintenance, billing authority, data access, dispute handling, regulatory changes, and termination rights.

Evaluating Whether an Electrical Support Program Fits Your Portfolio

An electrical support program deserves serious consideration when the building has a persistent bulk utility expense, recurring disputes about estimated charges, or limited visibility into unit consumption. It's also relevant when an owner is preparing for refinancing, a major upgrade, or a portfolio review and needs cleaner operating information.
Use this screening checklist:
Cost pressure:
Bulk electricity is compressing the property's operating performance.
Tenant friction:
Residents challenge charges because the allocation method is difficult to explain.
Operational capacity:
Staff don't have the time or specialist knowledge to run metering and billing internally.
Regulatory fit:
The jurisdiction permits the proposed arrangement, subject to the required approvals and standards.
Portfolio strategy:
The owner values consistent reporting across multiple properties.
Contract tolerance:
The owner is prepared to evaluate a long-term provider agreement rather than optimise only for the installation date.

Tenant communication should start early. Explain what will be measured, how common areas are treated, when statements will change, who handles questions, and what information residents will receive. Avoid promising that every bill will fall. The defensible promise is clearer measurement and a more accountable process.

Before contacting providers, gather the building's utility bills, suite count, electrical drawings, principal meter information, occupancy structure, common-area details, access constraints, current tenant billing rules, and known complaint history. Property teams that need help
interpreting an electrical assessment report
should resolve technical uncertainties before signing a project agreement.

Ask each provider to show the full chain, from compliance review through commissioning and monthly support. Compare ownership, term, billing authority, maintenance, data access, resident service, dispute handling, and exit provisions. The cheapest installation is rarely the cheapest operating model if the owner later inherits the hidden work.

Ask each provider to show the full chain, from compliance review through commissioning and monthly support. Compare ownership, term, billing authority, maintenance, data access, resident service, dispute handling, and exit provisions. The cheapest installation is rarely the cheapest operating model if the owner later inherits the hidden work.
